title: Vaccines & Antibiotic Resistance Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll get vaccinated, learn about herd immunity, and trace how antibiotic resistance evolves.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Immune Response — active and passive immunity, herd immunity, vaccines, and antibiotic resistance via natural selection.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Two ways to gain immunity.

Active immunity — your own immune system makes antibodies.
- Natural: catching the disease
- Artificial: vaccination

Slow to develop (days/weeks), but long-lasting because of memory cells.

Passive immunity — antibodies given to you.
- Natural: across placenta, in breast milk
- Artificial: antibody injection (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)

Fast, but short — no memory cells made.

Vaccines contain harmless antigens:
- Killed pathogen (whole-cell)
- Attenuated (weakened live)
- Subunit (just antigens)
- mRNA (cell makes the antigen)

They trigger a primary response + memory cells, without illness.

Herd immunity: if enough people are immune, pathogen can't spread between hosts → unvaccinated people (babies, immunocompromised) are also protected.

Threshold depends on R₀ (basic reproduction number). Measles needs ~95% coverage.

Antibiotics kill bacteria; viruses are unaffected.

By chance mutation, a few bacteria are resistant (e.g. produce β-lactamase that breaks penicillin).

When antibiotic is applied:
1. Susceptible bacteria die
2. Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
3. Population becomes mostly resistant — directional selection

MRSA and TB are infamous examples. To slow resistance: complete antibiotic courses, avoid overuse, develop new antibiotics, good hygiene.

It's not bacteria 'learning' — it's natural selection on pre-existing mutations.

options: Active natural

mcqs.q: How do bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic?
options: They learn to resist
Random mutations conferring resistance are selected for
Antibiotic damages their DNA usefully
They share resistance from animals only

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: Vaccines insert new genes into your DNA permanently.
Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.

mcqs.q: What is actually transferred to the body when you get a vaccine?
options: Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Antigens (often from weakened, dead, or fragmented pathogens) that train the immune system to make memory cells.
Vaccines insert new genes into your DNA permanently.
Vaccines inject ready-made antibodies directly into the bloodstream.
